canonical_statement: The IPD meta-analysis evaluated whether early SGLT2 inhibitor treatment in acute heart failure improves diuresis, in-hospital outcomes, and post-discharge outcomes.

Eligible studies were English-language randomized controlled trials of SGLT2 inhibitor therapy in acute or decompensated heart failure with placebo, usual-care, or other control therapy and available diuretic-response data.
The search retrieved 52 records, assessed 16 full texts, identified 8 unique studies, and included 6 RCTs in the harmonized IPD database after two studies could not contribute IPD.

population.label: Included RCTs in harmonized IPD database

canonical_statement: The pooled analysis included 623 patients, with 314 randomized to SGLT2 inhibitor therapy and 309 to placebo or control.

population.label: Pooled acute heart failure IPD population

canonical_statement: The pooled population had a median age of 67 years; 386 of 623 participants were male, corresponding to 38% female.

population.label: Pooled acute heart failure IPD population

canonical_statement: History of heart failure was reported in 473 of 623 patients (76%), and diabetes in 412 of 622 patients (66%).

population.label: Pooled acute heart failure IPD population

canonical_statement: Median LVEF was 35% (IQR 30% to 55%) among 554 participants with available data.
Median baseline eGFR was 52 mL/min/1.73 m2 (IQR 40 to 69) among 521 participants with available data.
Baseline loop diuretic use was reported in 491 of 623 patients (79%); the median baseline loop diuretic dose was 40 mg (IQR 10 to 80) among 250 patients with dose data.

canonical_statement: Empagliflozin was used in 100 treated participants; pooled trials used 10 mg or 25 mg regimens depending on the source trial.

canonical_statement: Five of six trials enrolled within 24 hours of admission; Tamaki et al. allowed inclusion within 96 hours. For the IPD analysis, Day 1 was standardized to the first day of study drug administration, which occurred on the admission day in 64% and within 48 hours in 93%.
The primary outcome was cumulative diuresis in millilitres at 24 hours.

outcome.definition: Cumulative urine output in millilitres at 24 hours after standardized study-drug Day 1.

canonical_statement: Clinical secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality and heart-failure rehospitalization at 30 and 60 days.

outcome.definition: Analyzed separately and as time to first composite event at 30 and 60 days.

canonical_statement: The hierarchical win-ratio endpoint prioritized time to all-cause mortality within 30 days, then heart-failure rehospitalization within 30 days, then 24-hour diuresis.

outcome.definition: Death within 30 days, HF rehospitalization within 30 days, then 24-hour diuresis, in that order.

canonical_statement: Follow-up availability varied by trial: two trials only supplied in-hospital mortality, EMPA-RESPONSE-AHF supplied 60-day follow-up, and EMPAG-HF and DICTATE-HF supplied 30-day follow-up.
For DAPA-RESPONSE-AHF, categorical events occurring on Days 0 to 30 were assigned to Day 30 and events occurring on Days 31 to 60 were assigned to Day 45 for Cox and Kaplan-Meier analyses.
Heart-failure rehospitalization data were available only from EMPA-RESPONSE-AHF, DICTATE-HF, and DAPA-RESPONSE-AHF, with DAPA-RESPONSE-AHF subject to categorical event-time constraints.

Safety analyses assessed hyperkalaemia and hypokalaemia on Days 2 and 3 after excluding patients with the corresponding baseline abnormality, plus several prespecified serum-creatinine worsening definitions.
Ketoacidosis and genital-tract infection data were too limited across included datasets for meaningful pooled analysis.
Primary analyses used linear, logistic, and Cox regression with original study modeled as a fixed effect; regression and proportional-hazards assumptions were checked before analysis.

Sensitivity analyses excluded trials with active controls, repeated main analyses with original study as a random effect, and performed study-level meta-analysis including an excluded trial when aggregate clinical outcome data were available.
The IPD meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO as CRD420250625357 and reported according to PRISMA-IPD guidance.
Five included trials were rated low risk of bias across assessed domains; the Ibrahim trial had some concerns for outcome measurement because outcome assessors knew treatment assignment.
Early SGLT2 inhibitor therapy increased 24-hour cumulative diuresis versus placebo/control; the adjusted between-group difference was 604 mL (95% CI 340 to 890).

canonical_statement: The pooled safety analysis found no significant between-group difference in the prespecified kidney-function worsening endpoints, while hypokalaemia was less frequent with SGLT2 inhibitor therapy at Days 2 and 3.

The authors concluded that early SGLT2 inhibitor initiation during acute-heart-failure admission increases diuresis without increasing natriuresis and reduces post-discharge mortality and HF readmission.

The authors argued that the findings support prompt SGLT2 inhibitor implementation upon hospital admission and described SGLT2 inhibitors as a cornerstone of contemporary acute-heart-failure management.

The discussion interprets the combination of greater diuresis without greater natriuresis as consistent with a contribution from glycosuria and osmotic diuresis rather than enhanced natriuresis alone.
Two identified trials could not contribute IPD, one because of European Union collaboration restrictions involving Russia and one because the original consent did not permit data sharing.
Included RCTs used heterogeneous comparator conditions, including placebo and active or usual-care controls.
Intervention duration, follow-up length, and collected outcomes varied across trials; not all trials systematically reported HF rehospitalization.
Important SGLT2 inhibitor adverse events such as genital infections and diabetic ketoacidosis were sparsely available, preventing a comprehensive pooled safety assessment.
Natriuresis data were not consistently available across trials.
The analysis could not adjust for loop-diuretic dose during treatment because these data were limited, leaving a potential confounder of decongestive response unmodeled.
Residual between-study heterogeneity and the small number of included trials may limit generalizability.
No funding was acquired for the individual patient-level meta-analysis.
The authors state that data are available upon reasonable request.
Several authors reported consulting, speaker, grant, research-support, or honoraria relationships with pharmaceutical or medical-device companies; all other authors reported no relevant disclosures.
The authors disclosed use of ChatGPT4.0 for drafting and coding assistance and stated that generative-AI use was verified and redacted as necessary.

The main-text Table 3 reports adjusted P=.053 for Day-2 weight change, whereas Supplementary Table S7 reports fixed-effect-model P=.008 for the same group medians; the source does not explain the discrepancy.

Supplementary Table S5 prints HR 0.32 with 95% CI 0.38 to 1.35 for the NT-proBNP >=3340 ng/L subgroup, placing the point estimate outside its printed interval; the value was not normalized into a quantitative subgroup atom.

Table 1 prints the EMPAG-HF placebo urine-output IQR as 6450 to 3550 mL, with the lower bound larger than the upper bound; that secondary-reported trial result was not converted into a quantitative atom.

The subgroup-methods prose prints the eGFR cutoff unit as mg/ml/1.73 m2, while Table 2 and Supplementary Table S5 use the conventional filtration-rate unit mL/min/1.73 m2; the discrepancy was retained rather than silently repaired.

Supplementary Table S6 reports placebo-only 24-hour diuresis medians of 2250 mL with SGLT2i and 3050 mL with placebo, yet P=.005 without a reported effect estimate; this direction differs from the full-cohort raw medians, so no comparative quantitative atom was created for that row.
